chapter.title: 1 A.M.
chapter.sub: It works at one in the morning. Nobody writes it down.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the season map ahead of its production-bible entry · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 2 · EPISODE 9 · DRAFT  Teach-back · Maya, and Priya by phone · Level L3  Riverbend Festival, load-in night. Three thousand people at the gates at nine; the headliner's stream tomorrow night. At 12:58 a.m., half the ticket scanners and the stream go dark.  ⚑ RV-55: addresses and DHCP behavior are illustrative, and the workaround in this episode is deliberately flawed. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: It Works at One in the Morning
items.stakes: Three thousand people at the gates at nine. The scanners and the stream went down in the same minute. The people who changed it went home.
items.clock: Eight hours to gates. Four hours of sleep, if you're lucky.
items.reward: Twelve green lanes. A promise to write it down.

objectives.text: Separate the networks in thirty seconds
Find the two answers to one question
Decide who fixes someone else's network
Look closer: two notes nobody finished

items.rumor: Somewhere in this story is a napkin. It will matter in two years.

items.alt: The festival site at night under work lights: a row of gate kiosks, every other one showing a red screen. The ticketing lead points at them. Maya arrives running.

bubbles.text: Half my scanners just went offline. Full Wi-Fi bars. Three thousand people at nine.
And my stream test just dropped. Same minute.

items.caption: Gates at 9:00 a.m. The headliner's stream tomorrow night. Eight hours, and nobody's slept.

items.alt: The network tent. On a folding table: our AV switch and router, and the site's switch, now joined by a new yellow patch cable tagged SHARE INTERNET.

bubbles.text: They patched it at 12:40 and went home. I told them to ask you.
Two networks. One cable. Eighteen minutes.

items.caption: What changed? A yellow cable with a helpful label.

items.alt: Flashback, 12:40 a.m.: two site network techs plug the yellow cable between the switches, pleased with themselves, jackets already on.

bubbles.text: Share internet. Easy. They'll thank us in the morning.
Tag it so Maya knows. We're off.

items.caption: A kind gesture, a real change, and nobody who owned it still on site.

items.title: “SHARED INTERNET — THEY'LL THANK US :)”
items.body: A kindness, written by someone who went home. The smiley face is the only part of this night that is still correct at 1 a.m.

items.prompt: 12:59. Scanners half offline, stream dropping, a new cable between two networks. Thirty seconds.
items.happening: Two networks were patched together 18 minutes ago; since then half the scanners and the stream fail.
items.risk: Three thousand ticket holders; tomorrow's headliner stream.
timeout: The ticketing lead starts power-cycling scanners one by one. Some come back, some don't, and nobody knows why.
When a change breaks things, undo the change — your end of it — first.

hints.text: What changed — and which end of it is yours?

options.label: Predict, then unplug the patch at our switch
options.result: Prediction: scanners recover, our stream loses internet. Both happen. The ticketing lead reconnects her scanners: every one goes green.
options.consequence: Separation restored. You're back to one problem: we have no internet.

options.label: Reboot the site's switch
options.result: Imani catches your arm. “That's theirs.” If it had rebooted, its table of who-has-what would be gone.
options.consequence: Not your device, and the evidence would go with it.
options.fail: Someone else's network, and it erases what happened.

options.label: Call Priya first
options.result: She answers on the sixth ring. “Is anything unplugged yet?”
options.consequence: Useful — after the one move you already know.

options.label: Tell the site team to fix it
options.result: Voicemail. They're asleep in a hotel twenty minutes away.
options.consequence: It's their network; they're not here.
options.fail: Handing it back to people who aren't there isn't a plan.

items.alt: Maya unplugs the yellow patch at our switch. A status board shows twelve of twelve scanners online.
items.caption: Separation restored. The scanners are fine. Our stream has no internet — it never did on its own.

items.alt: Two scanner screens side by side from the ticketing lead's photos at 12:58. The working one: IP 10.20.0.37, gateway 10.20.0.254. The failing one: IP 10.20.0.142, gateway 10.20.0.1.
items.caption: Same network, same Wi-Fi, different gateways. One of those gateways is our router.

items.alt: Left, the site's network sheet taped to their rack: 10.20.0.0/24, gateway .254, DHCP .10 to .250. Right, our AV router's label: 10.20.0.1, DHCP on, .100 to .199.
items.caption: Both teams picked the same private range. Both routers hand out addresses.

items.title: Two answers to one question.
items.body: The yellow cable made one flat network with two DHCP servers on it. Every scanner that asked “what's my address and where's the door out?” believed whichever server answered first. The site's said “.254 — here's the internet.” Ours said “.1” — a router with no internet. And the site's server, not knowing our encoder lived at .50, handed .50 to a scanner. One cable, two failures, one cause.
items.label: Test: reason from the two servers before you read on.

items.alt: System View: one address bar for 10.20.0.0/24 with the site's DHCP pool .10–.250 and the AV pool .100–.199 overlapping; the encoder's fixed .50 also leased to a scanner. Two routers: .254 to the internet, .1 to nowhere.
items.caption: Two servers, one range: half the scanners got the wrong door, and the encoder lost its address.

items.alt: The encoder's event log on a laptop: 12:31 stream test OK; 12:58 address conflict, 10.20.0.50 answered by another device; uplink lost.
items.caption: The stream and the scanners were one fault wearing two costumes.

items.label: **First failure point:** a scanner with full bars that can't check a ticket.

items.alt: Maya sits alone on a road case in the tent, head down, laptop closed on her knees.
items.caption: She knows audio. She knows radio. At one in the morning, this is somebody else's language — and it's her stream.

lines.text: (Audio, she knows. Radio, she knows. At one in the morning this is somebody else's language — and it's her stream.)

items.prompt: 1:12. You need shared internet for the stream, and the site's router has its admin password taped to the case. Who fixes this?
items.happening: Separated: scanners fine, no internet for the stream.

options.label: Log in with the taped password and fix their DHCP
options.result: Their router, their pool, your hands. It might work. The site lead wakes to a network someone else redesigned.
options.consequence: You'd own a system you don't understand and aren't allowed to touch.
options.fail: A password on a case isn't permission. It's their network.

options.label: Text the site lead what happened, then call Priya
options.result: The text goes into a sleeping phone: joined at 12:40, two DHCP servers, we unplugged our end. Priya answers from her kitchen.
options.consequence: The owner has the facts. Someone who knows more than you is on the line.

options.label: Wait until the site lead wakes at seven
options.result: Separated, safe, and the stream has no internet until at least seven.
options.consequence: Gates are fine; the stream test waits; nothing gets learned.

options.label: Plug the patch back in and hope it settles
options.result: Half the scanners go red again within a minute.

items.alt: Maya's phone: a text to the site network lead at 1:13 — your team joined our AV switch to yours at 12:40; two DHCP servers on one network; half the scanners lost internet; we unplugged our end only; call me.
items.caption: The owner is asleep. The owner still hears it first, in writing.

items.alt: Split panel. Left: Maya in the network tent on the phone. Right: Priya in her kitchen at night, phone to her ear, a mug on the counter.

bubbles.text: Two networks, same range, two DHCP servers. I unplugged our end. Scanners fine, stream has no internet.
Good. Evidence, not theories. Now: whose network, and who's awake?

items.where: on the phone · Priya's kitchen, again

lines.text: Evidence, not theories. Now tell it back to me.
…Their DHCP only. Ours off. Our gear on .240 up.
Good. Now go to sleep before you tell it back to me wrong.

items.sub: Beginner · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Priya and Maya beside a board. A subnet is a block of addresses that can talk directly. DHCP hands out addresses automatically. A static address is typed in by hand. How many devices fit? Two to the thirty-two minus the prefix, minus two. A slash-twenty-six: two to the six is sixty-four, minus two — sixty-two devices.

bubbles.text: A subnet is a block of addresses that can talk directly. DHCP hands out addresses automatically. A static address is typed in by hand.
How many devices fit?
Two to the thirty-two minus the prefix, minus two. A slash-twenty-six: two to the six is sixty-four, minus two — sixty-two devices.

items.caption: Beginner: the term, what it means, the formula — and one worked example out loud.

items.text: 📘 RAY'S NOTEBOOK · BEGINNER  Terms    Subnet   A block of addresses that can talk to each other directly, written with a prefix like /24.   DHCP   The automatic service that hands out addresses from a range.   Static address   An address typed into a device by hand, not handed out automatically.   Formula, variables and a worked example   ƒ FORMULA · Usable hosts in a subnet  hosts = 2 (32 − prefix)  − 2   prefix  the /number (e.g. /24)  − 2  network and broadcast addresses can't be hosts    Worked example.  A /26: 2⁶ − 2 = 62 usable hosts.
📒 EMPATHIA LEARN FIELDBOOK · MODULE 20 OF 31 · PP. 28–31  PART 2 AV NETWORKING & DATA  Page 31:  and document it . Maya underlined it at 1 a.m., then closed the book.

items.label: **Fieldbook module 20 — Addresses, subnets and the IP plan.** Beginner support: every new word is defined, and every formula comes with its variables and a worked example.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · module 20 · tap a plate to open it full size     AV networking 101     AV networking — the church network     AV networking — a typical AV network     Mid-level AV networking

items.label: **Learn it now:** addressing, DHCP and fixed addresses.

items.prompt: Priya: “It's their network and they asked to share. Tonight you only change your side. Pick.” Twenty-five seconds.
items.happening: Priya lays out the options for sharing the site's internet tonight.
known: ◉ Site pool: .10–.250, fills from the bottom
◉ Our router's DHCP is ours to switch off
unknown: Whether the site's server checks for conflicts
items.risk: Tomorrow's headliner stream; the gates if you get it wrong.
timeout: Priya waits, then: “Maya. It's one-twenty. Pick one and tell it back to me.”
At 1 a.m. the clock is your judgment, not the gates.

hints.text: Only one server should answer. Which one can you switch off?

items.lab_label: now do it properly — the version somebody could have written down.

options.label: Turn our DHCP off; give our gear fixed addresses at the top of the range; rejoin; text the owner
options.result: One server answers now — theirs. Encoder .240, console .241, stage boxes .242–.245.
options.consequence: Scanners stay green, the stream gets internet. Priya: “Now tell me what's wrong with it.”

options.label: Rejoin as it was and restart everything
options.result: Two servers again. Half the scanners go red.
options.consequence: The same failure with fresh leases.
options.fail: Restarting doesn't remove the second server.

options.label: Fixed addresses in the middle of the range, .50–.90
options.result: The site's pool is already leasing those. Two conflicts before you finish typing.
options.fail: The busy middle of someone else's pool is the worst place to squat.

options.label: Stay separated; stream over the bonded cellular unit
options.result: The unit shows one bar in the valley. Tomorrow's headliner at 2 Mbit/s, maybe.
options.consequence: Safe for the gates; a gamble for the stream.

items.title: The server that answers the question
items.body: In October 1993 the Internet Engineering Task Force published the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, building on an older bootstrap protocol from 1985. Instead of someone typing an address, a gateway and a name server into every machine, a server could lease them from a pool for a set time. It made networks you could simply plug into. It also made one rule matter more than ever: on one network, one server answers that question — or several servers answer it by a clearly agreed plan.

items.alt: Our AV router's settings: DHCP off; encoder fixed at 10.20.0.240, console at .241, stage boxes at .242 to .245. Maya points at the screen.
items.caption: Every change is on our side of the cable. Every change goes in the text to the site lead.

items.alt: Split panel, Priya now on the left explaining, Maya on the right listening.

bubbles.text: Why the top? Their pool hands out from the bottom. Sixty scanners. You're nowhere near .240 — tonight.
Tell it back: their DHCP only. Ours off. Our gear on .240 up. Rejoin. Test gates, then stream.

items.caption: The teach-back: say it in your own words before you do it.

items.alt: System View of the workaround: one DHCP server, the site's; our gear fixed at .240–.249, drawn inside the site's pool; tonight's sixty leases fill only the bottom of the pool. A red dashed box: our fixed addresses are inside their pool, not excluded.
items.caption: Look at where the green sits.

items.alt: The gate kiosks, every screen green. The ticketing lead grins. Maya's phone, on cellular, shows the stream's private preview playing live.

bubbles.text: Twenty test tickets, every lane. All green.

items.caption: Proof where the users are: the gates, and a phone that isn't on either network.

items.title: The fix has a fuse.
items.body: Priya's question — “now tell me what's wrong with it” — has an answer. Our fixed addresses sit inside the site's pool, and the site's server was never told to leave them alone. Tonight the pool fills from the bottom and sixty scanners never get near .240. On a bigger site, a busier day, or a building with hundreds of rooms, the server will one day hand .240 to someone else. It works because the place is small. That is not the same as being right.
items.label: Test: when does it fail, and whose fix is the real one?

items.alt: Split panel again: Priya, tired, serious; Maya listening.

bubbles.text: At seven, you and the site lead reserve those addresses — or separate the networks properly. And write this down tonight.
Tonight. Promise.

items.alt: 1:42 a.m. Imani arrives in the tent with two coffees; Maya has her notebook open to a blank page.

bubbles.text: It works? Then we're done. Make it work, write it up tomorrow. Gates at nine; you need four hours' sleep.
Priya said write it now.

items.caption: Imani protects the show. Sometimes that means protecting it from its own paperwork.

items.prompt: It works. We're done. Make it work, write it up tomorrow. You need four hours' sleep.

options.label: “Priya said write it now. Two minutes.”
options.reply: Two minutes. Go. I'm holding your coffee hostage.

options.label: (Write it on the napkin under your coffee.)

items.prompt: 1:43. Imani is holding your coffee and your jacket. The page is blank. Twenty seconds.
items.happening: The workaround works; the owner of the fix is asleep; the crew lead says tomorrow.
known: ◉ The site lead hasn't seen it
unknown: Whether tomorrow will have a spare ten minutes
items.risk: Whoever inherits this network — and whatever it gets copied into.
timeout: Imani takes the notebook out of your hands and closes it. “Tomorrow.”
When you don't choose, the tiredest person in the tent chooses.

hints.text: Where would a record be both findable and durable?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S02E09). The printed story follows Imani's “tomorrow.” It isn't the right call — it's the one that happened.

options.label: Write it up now, properly, in the shared log
options.result: Imani: “Maya. Bed.” You compromise: three lines on a paper napkin — ours DHCP off, gear .240–.249 inside their pool, fix with site lead at 7.
options.consequence: The napkin goes in your jacket pocket. (It will not survive tomorrow night's rain.)

options.label: Imani's call: “Tomorrow.”
options.result: You close the notebook on a blank page. At seven the site lead is busy with gates; at noon you're doing RF; tomorrow becomes the day after.
options.consequence: Nobody writes it down. The workaround starts to look like the design. (DEBT-003)

options.label: “It works. There's nothing to write.”
options.consequence: A workaround nobody remembers is a design nobody chose.
options.fail: “It works” is the most dangerous sentence in operations.

options.label: Save Priya's steps in the notes on your RF laptop
options.result: Quick, private, and only on that laptop.
options.consequence: Remember where the RF file lives.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #20 · AVERY'S LENS  Make it reversible, then write it down  Changes people can undo — and understand later — are safer changes.  The 1 a.m. workaround worked, and nobody could undo or explain it the next day.

items.alt: Close on Maya's notebook: a page titled Riverbend · Network, and nothing under it. The notebook is closing.
items.caption: DEBT-003: the workaround nobody wrote down.

items.title: Four lines in biro
items.body: *their DHCP / ours OFF / our kit .240–.249 (in THEIR pool!!) / reserve at 7am.* The two exclamation marks are the only warning anyone ever wrote about it. The napkin goes into a jacket pocket. The jacket goes into the rain in a week.

items.alt: Grey morning, 7:04. Maya on the phone to the site lead's voicemail again; Ben waves her toward the stage for the RF walk test.

bubbles.text: …it's Maya again, about the addresses — call me when you're —
RF walk. Now. The headliner's crew lands at ten.

items.caption: At seven the site lead is at the gates. At noon Maya is doing RF. Tomorrow becomes the day after.

items.alt: Morning. The gates open under a grey sky; a crowd streams through, every kiosk screen green.
items.caption: 9:00 a.m. Three thousand people, twelve green lanes. Nobody in line will ever know about 1 a.m.

items.label: **Service Mode:** it's 12:58 a.m. Your network, their network, one yellow cable.
**Class match:** where did each festival fault really live?

items.alt: Mid-morning. The ticketing lead and Imani by the gate tent, relieved.

bubbles.text: Smoothest gate we've had. Whatever you did at one o'clock, keep doing it.
We will.

items.caption: Nobody says: “Where is it written down?”

lines.text: (Nobody asks where it's written down. That's the dark part. Nobody asks.)

items.alt: Afternoon. Ben, the rigging and staging lead, in his white hard hat, holds up his phone to show a forecast: rain after 9 p.m. The headliner is at 9:15.

bubbles.text: Rain after nine tomorrow. Headliner's on at nine-fifteen. Everybody reads the weather plan tonight. Everybody.

items.caption: Next: *Festival in the Rain.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  When two networks are joined and things break, undo the join on your side first. Then read the addresses and gateways: one network needs one DHCP server, and fixed addresses belong outside the pool or reserved in it. A network has an owner even at 1 a.m. — tell them in writing. And a workaround that works because the place is small is a fuse, not a fix: write down what you did, why, what's wrong with it and who fixes it, before you sleep.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Imani was kind, tired and wrong, and Maya let her be. Think of a “tomorrow” in your own work that never came. What would it have cost to write three lines?  Boundary: this reflection proves nothing about the network.
